question: What are VLMs, how are they trained and how should they be evaluated, as an entry point for newcomers to the field?
contributions: Four training paradigms for VLMs: contrastive, masking, generative, pretrained backbones (s2)
A guide to VLM training: data, software, compute, model choice, grounding, alignment, text-rich images, PEFT (s3)
Evaluation approaches: visio-linguistic benchmarks, bias, hallucination, memorization, red teaming (s4)

results.claim: MiniGPT-4 trains only the linear projection, in two rounds; round one is 20k steps at batch 256.
results.setup: Round 1: ~5M pairs from Conceptual Caption, SBU, LAION; BLIP-2 visual encoder and Vicuna reused off the shelf
results.quote: The first involves 20k training steps (with a batch size of 256), corresponding to around 5M image-text pairs

results.claim: MiniGPT-4 round one took about ten hours on four A100s.
results.value: four A100 GPUs for around ten hours
results.setup: Linear projection only trained
results.quote: The authors only used four A100 GPUs for around ten hours

results.claim: MiniGPT-4 round two (curated instruction-format data) needed 400 steps at batch 12.
results.setup: Second round of linear-projection training
results.quote: needing only 400 training steps (with a batch size of 12)

results.claim: LLaVA 1.5 is trained on 600k image-text pairs and takes about a day on 8 A100s.
results.setup: MLP projector plus academic VQA instruction data; frozen/trainable split not stated by Bordes
results.quote: LLava 1.5 is trained on 600k image-text pairs making it much more efficient to train compared to other instruction-tuned models such as InstructBLIP or Qwen-VL. Training takes approximately one day on 8-A100 GPUs.

results.claim: Frozen keeps the 7B language model frozen, which the authors call crucial; vision encoder and linear map are trained from scratch; performance modest.
results.setup: NF-ResNet-50 encoder; text generation objective on Conceptual Captions
results.quote: is kept frozen (this is crucial to maintain the features that the pre-trained model had already learned)

results.claim: BLIP-2 trains only a Q-Former mapper between frozen pretrained models.
results.setup: Frozen vision encoder (such as CLIP) and frozen LLM (such as OPT)
results.quote: A relatively small (∼100-200M parameters) component called a Q-Former is trained for this mapping

results.claim: Full fine-tuning of pretrained models becomes impractical as they grow; PEFT falls in four groups (LoRA, prompt, adapter, mapping).
results.setup: Stated as motivation for PEFT; conditional on growing model size, no memory or cost figure given
results.quote: As the size of pre-trained models continues to grow, fine-tuning the entire parameter set of these models becomes impractical due to computational constraints.

results.claim: VL-adapter with weight-sharing rivals full fine-tuning while updating 4.18% (image-text) and 3.39% (video-text) of parameters.
results.setup: Unified multi-task framework over image-text and video-text benchmarks
results.quote: (4.18% for image-text tasks and 3.39% for video-text tasks)

results.claim: VPT adds under 1% of parameters in the input space with backbone frozen; accuracy comparable or better than full fine-tuning in many instances.
results.setup: Large vision Transformers, not VLMs
results.quote: VPT introduces a minimal amount (less than 1% of model parameters) of trainable parameters in the input space.

results.claim: QLoRA backpropagates through a frozen 4-bit quantized LM into LoRA weights.
results.setup: Described for language models; no memory figure given
results.quote: back-propagation of gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pre-trained language model into LoRA

results.claim: Mapping-based methods keep both modules frozen and need fewer trainable parameters and less data; a per-feature linear map (LiMBeR) makes the LLM sequence as long as the visual feature count.
results.source: Merullo et al. 2022; Mañas et al. 2023; Vallaeys et al. 2024
results.setup: LiMBeR versus MAPL (learnable query tokens)
results.quote: the length of the sequence passed to the LLM is the same as the number of visual feature vectors, increasing the computational cost of training and inference

results.claim: Training a contrastive CLIP-like model on hundreds of millions of images from scratch should need no more than 64 GPUs, about 10K USD (authors' estimate).
results.setup: Requires a high-quality dataset and masking strategies on bigger models; an estimate, not a reported run
results.quote: should not require more than 64 GPUs (which should be equivalent to spending around 10K USD in compute)

results.claim: OpenCLIP was trained on 256 to 600 GPUs across days or weeks.
results.setup: Depending on model size
results.quote: was trained using between 256 and 600 GPUs across multiple days or weeks depending on the model size

results.claim: From-scratch VLM training needs hundreds to thousands of GPUs and hundreds of millions of image-text pairs.
results.setup: General statement motivating pretrained backbones
results.quote: They often require hundreds to thousands of GPUs while having to use hundreds of millions of images and text pairs.

results.claim: Resolution, visual encoder capacity and visual pretraining data matter most; how modalities are connected matters much less.
results.setup: Zero-shot classification and VQA; second-hand report
results.quote: image resolution, visual encoder capacity, and visual pretraining data are the choices that most impact model performance

results.claim: In binary-caption benchmarks a model with all-zero parameters could reach 100% accuracy because argmax returns the first element and the correct caption is often first.
results.setup: Benchmarks that discriminate a correct caption from a negative; ties not handled
results.quote: a model whose parameters are all equal to zero could achieve 100% accuracy in these benchmarks

results.claim: The original VQA benchmark is solvable blind: questions starting with 'Is there a clock' have answer 'yes' 98% of the time.
results.setup: Original VQA (Antol et al. 2015)
results.quote: has the answer “yes” 98% of the time

results.claim: VQA Accuracy (exact string match) is too stringent and underestimates current VLM systems in generative and OOD settings.
results.setup: Settings: free-form generation and OOD evaluation; it worked well for multiple-choice and IID
results.quote: the traditional VQA Accuracy metric is too stringent and tends to underestimate the performance of current VLM systems

results.claim: Human fine-grained annotation is costly so datasets are small, suiting evaluation or fine-tuning more than pretraining.
results.setup: Authors' judgement about detailed annotations (e.g. DCI)
results.quote: the number of images with highly detailed annotations is often low which makes often those datasets more suited for evaluation or fine-tuning than for large-scale pre-training

results.claim: LLaVAR: adding text-rich instruction data gave up to 20% accuracy gain on text-based VQA.
results.setup: LLaVA base; 422K LAION text-rich images OCRed, 16K GPT-4 conversations; slight gain on natural images
results.quote: with up to a 20% accuracy improvement on text-based VQA datasets and a slight improvement on natural images

results.claim: LLaVA-RLHF reaches 94% of GPT-4 on LLaVA-Bench and beats baselines by 60% on MMHal-Bench.
results.setup: Baselines and metric not named by Bordes
results.quote: LLaVA-RLHF achieves 94% performance level of GPT-4 [Achiam et al., 2023]. On MMHAL-BENCH with a special focus on penalizing hallucinations, LLaVA-RLHF outperforms baselines by 60%.

results.claim: Instruction-tuning sets are much smaller than pretraining data.
results.setup: Unit after 'few' is not given
results.quote: instruction tuning data sizes ranging from a few to one hundred thousand samples
results.note: MIMIC-IT (~2.8M) and LLaVA (150k) are cited on p26-27 and exceed this stated range.

results.claim: MIMIC-IT has around 2.8M instruction-response pairs; OpenFlamingo tuned on it gives Otter.
results.setup: With in-context examples
results.quote: around 2.8M multimodal instruction-response pairs with in-context examples

results.claim: LLaVA used 150k synthetically generated visual instruction samples.
results.setup: Vicuna + CLIP ViT-L/14 with linear projector
results.quote: The authors generate 150k synthetically generated visual instruction samples for fine-tuning.

results.claim: Zero-shot VLM performance depends mostly on how often the concepts appear in training data.
results.setup: Estimated by recognition model (RAM) over training data
results.quote: the zero-shot performances of VLMs depend mostly on how much those zero-shot downstream concepts are present in the training data

results.claim: Current VLMs are not better than random chance on spatial relations in a controlled synthetic test.
results.setup: PUG synthetic scenes; animal moved left or right
results.quote: current VLMs are not performing better than random chance when evaluating spatial relations

results.claim: Text randomization (masking a random fraction of caption tokens each epoch) was the most effective regularizer against memorization.
results.setup: CLIP models; deja vu memorization measured as target vs reference model k-NN gap
results.quote: find text randomization to be the most effective regularization technique that significantly reduces memorization without severely penalizing the model utility

results.claim: Randomly masking image tokens speeds training and improves performance.
results.setup: Large image-text models
results.quote: by randomly masking image tokens one can significantly speed up training time while improving model performances

results.claim: Most MM-LLMs limit inputs to 224 x 224; Monkey reaches up to 1344x896 with LoRA-tuned encoder and trainable resampler.
results.setup: Sliding-window patches processed independently
results.quote: This allows Monkey to handle higher resolutions up to 1344×896 pixels

results.claim: Synthetic captions help CLIP pretraining but their gain is capped at scale by low caption diversity.
results.setup: Mixture of real and BLIP2 synthetic captions
results.quote: the improvement provided by synthetic captions is capped by the limited diversity of generated captions

results.claim: A 24 fps video needs 24x storage/processing if each frame is treated as an image.
results.setup: Per-frame treatment of video
results.quote: a 24 fps video requires 24× storage/processing, if each frame is considered as an image

limits: Authors say it 'should not be considered as a survey or a complete guide on VLMs' and cite only select works (p4).
Nearly every number is second-hand from a cited paper; no experiment of its own.
No learning rates, epochs, optimizer, LoRA rank/target modules, VRAM figures, minimum dataset size, holdout or in-training monitoring guidance for fine-tuning a VLM.
No procedure for deciding what to freeze when adapting an existing VLM; only Frozen's rationale (p15) and a general note that pretrained backbones suit limited compute (p24).
No head-to-head of LoRA vs adapters vs mapping on one task.
Authors concede there is no holistic way to evaluate multimodal/interleaved data quality (p21) and that many benchmarks have severe limitations (p46).
v1 of May 2024; model lineup, 224x224 resolution norm and cost estimate date from then.
practices: Prune and deduplicate image-text data; duplicates waste compute and risk memorization (Fig 2 caption p17).
Use a pretrained image encoder and/or LLM and learn only a mapping when compute is limited (s3.3.4, p24).
Store uncompressed files or use FFCV to relieve data-loading bottlenecks (p22).
Randomly mask image tokens to speed up training (p22).
Add a small random epsilon or track ties when scoring binary caption benchmarks (p37).
Check whether a benchmark is solvable from language alone before trusting it (s4.2.3, p40).
Pick text-centric benchmarks by the purpose of the evaluation (p35).
Consider LLM judges for VQA instead of exact-match accuracy (p34).
Apply text randomization as regularizer against memorization (p41).

terms.definition: the ability to correctly map text with visual clues
how well a VLM can abstain from answering questions it would otherwise get incorrect, and achieve high accuracy on questions it chooses to answer
fine-tuning a vision-language model on supervised data containing instructions, inputs, and the desired response
evaluating a model on a classification task for which the model was not explicitly trained
training only a mapping between pretrained unimodal modules while keeping them completely frozen and free of adapter layers
